section.title: Discovery problems and projects
section.p: The dashboard story has given us four ways to talk about the same motion:

Before we build the formal language of limits, it is worth testing those ideas. The problems in this section are not only practice. They are small investigations. Each one asks you to read a graph, build a trip, or discover a pattern that will return later in a more precise form.

subsection.title: Read a trip from a speed graph
subsection.p: The graph below records the velocity of a car over 6 hours. Velocity is measured in miles per hour. Positive velocity means the car moves in the chosen positive direction; negative velocity means it moves backward.

figure.caption: Each rectangle gives one signed change in position. Rectangles above the axis count positive; rectangles below the axis count negative.

paragraphs.title: Project
paragraphs.p: Starting from s(0)=0, answer the following questions.

li.p: Compute the signed change in position on each time interval.
Sketch the graph of s(t). It should be made of straight line segments.
Find the displacement from t=0 to t=6.
Find the total distance traveled from t=0 to t=6.
Find the average velocity and the average speed over the whole trip.

paragraphs.p: The total distance traveled is different. For total distance, the backward part adds positively:
The same trip has two averages because displacement and distance traveled answer different questions.

note.p: Displacement asks: Where did you end compared with where you started?
Distance traveled asks: How much road did you cover?

subsection.title: Design two different trips with the same displacement
subsection.p: A displacement is only a net result. It does not determine the whole trip.
Here are two different velocity histories on the interval 0\leq t\leq 4.

figure.caption: Two different velocity histories can have the same displacement. Signed area preserves the net change, not the full story.

paragraphs.title: Your turn
paragraphs.p: Design two new trips on 0\leq t\leq 5 that both have displacement 100 miles, but different total distances traveled.
One trip may use constant velocity. The other should include at least one interval of negative velocity.

li.p: What is the velocity function for each trip?
What is the displacement of each trip?
What is the total distance traveled by each trip?
Which graph gives a better story of what the driver actually did: the velocity graph or the final displacement alone?

paragraphs.p: The last question matters. Calculus often compresses a whole history into one number. That number is useful, but it is not the whole story.

exercise.title: Why can two different trips share a displacement?

statement.p: One discovery task asks you to design two different trips with the same displacement. In your own words, why is that possible, and what does a successful pair of trips show about signed area?

hint.p: Displacement cares about net change of position, not about the particular forward and backward pieces that produced it.

subsection.title: A changing slope needs nearness
subsection.p: The finite examples in this chapter had flat velocity pieces and straight position pieces. Their slopes were easy to read.
Curved graphs force a sharper question.

This is the first glimpse of the precise language of limits. A limit is not a guess from a table. It is a promise:
subsection.md: \text{make the input close enough, and the output becomes as close as required.}
subsection.p: For this example, the promise is easy because the error is exactly |h|. In more difficult examples, the whole task is to control the error.

To do that carefully, we need a language for distance on the number line, intervals around a point, functions, graphs, and eventually limits. The next chapter builds that language. It may look like a review at first, but it is not a detour. It is the measuring tape calculus needs.

exercise.title: What promise is a limit making?

statement.p: In the average-velocity example, the error was exactly |h|, so requiring |h|<0.01 made the average within 0.01 of 4. In your own words, what promise is a limit making, and why is that promise stronger than reading a number from a table?

hint.p: A table shows a few nearby values. A limit claims that every required closeness can be achieved by making the input close enough.
